source_title: Old Spice: Smell Like A Man, Man (Wieden+Kennedy campaign case)
publisher_issuer: Wieden+Kennedy (agency of record, first-party campaign case write-up); corroborated by multiple published case studies and Effie Awards documentation
company_context: Old Spice, a Procter & Gamble men's grooming brand, was perceived as dated and losing relevance in the men's body-wash category. In February 2010, P&G and agency Wieden+Kennedy launched 'The Man Your Man Could Smell Like' (featuring Isaiah Mustafa), a marketing-led repositioning aimed in part at female purchasers, who research showed bought a majority of men's body wash.
business_type: Consumer packaged goods (men's grooming / personal care brand)
geography: United States (primary market for reported results)
time_period: Calendar 2010 (campaign launch February 2010; sales results May-July 2010)
macro_context: Mature, commoditized personal-care category; rise of social/viral video marketing (YouTube, Twitter); insight that women purchase a majority of men's body wash reshaping the targeting strategy.
evidence_summary: A marketing-led repositioning reversed weak demand for a tired brand. Against an original goal of increasing body-wash sales by roughly 15%, Old Spice Red Zone body wash unit sales rose about 60% year over year by May 2010 and had more than doubled (up about 125% year over year) by July 2010, an all-time high for the brand, which became the number-one men's body wash in the U.S. The campaign also generated outsized engagement (the top commercial channel on YouTube, hundreds of millions to over a billion impressions, and large social-following growth), demonstrating that the demand turnaround was marketing-driven.

source_backed_metrics.body_wash_sales_growth_july_2010_yoy: approximately 125% (sales more than doubled; all-time high)
source_backed_metrics.market_position_outcome: number-one men's body wash in the U.S.
source_backed_metrics.campaign_launch: February 2010 ('The Man Your Man Could Smell Like', Isaiah Mustafa)

owner_decision_context: P&G and Wieden+Kennedy chose a bold creative repositioning that explicitly targeted the female buyer of men's body wash, betting that humor-led viral content plus a clear purchase-driver insight could revive a stagnant brand without competing purely on price.
action_taken: Launched and amplified 'The Man Your Man Could Smell Like' across TV, YouTube, and social media (including the follow-up real-time response videos), repositioning the brand and driving trial and repeat purchase.
outcome_evidence: Sales rose ~60% by May 2010 and ~125% (more than doubled) by July 2010 versus a ~15% goal, with Old Spice becoming the #1 U.S. men's body wash, confirming the marketing action drove a demand turnaround.
source_limitations: Primary corporate (P&G) shipment data is not publicly broken out at this granularity; the percentage figures derive from agency (Wieden+Kennedy) and widely republished case-study/Effie Awards sources reporting Nielsen-attributed data, not from an audited filing. Figures are directionally consistent across multiple independent published accounts but are not SEC-verified. A longer-run sustained-share figure circulated in secondary blogs (e.g., a ~27% figure) was ambiguous across sources and is therefore omitted.
directly_stated: The original goal was to increase body-wash sales by approximately 15%
By May 2010 Old Spice Red Zone body wash sales were up approximately 60% year over year
By July 2010 sales had more than doubled (up approximately 125% year over year), an all-time high
Old Spice became the number-one men's body wash in the U.S.
The campaign launched in February 2010 featuring Isaiah Mustafa (Wieden+Kennedy)
inferred: The gap between the ~15% goal and the ~125% actual indicates a marketing intervention that materially exceeded expectations in reversing weak demand
A demand turnaround achieved through repositioning rather than discounting is best classified as good-action-then-improvement addressing a demand-generation problem
why_useful_for_opsiq: A marketing-led, non-price demand turnaround for a mature CPG brand, useful for testing whether the engine can attribute improvement to a go-to-market/creative intervention addressing a demand-generation failure rather than to operations or pricing. The buyer-insight (women buying men's products) is a clean strategic-correction signal.
